title: Why do we yawn?
subtitle: Body & brain
subject: sciences
description: Everyone yawns: humans, dogs, sometimes even fetuses. It's probably not for "lack of oxygen". Here are the strongest leads.

hero.hook: You yawn. Your neighbor yawns. And it’s (almost) not contagious by chance.

blocks.text: Yawning seems commonplace. However, it is a complex reflex: jaw, thorax, diaphragm, the whole body gets involved. Lions, dogs, humans: many animals yawn.
For a long time, we said: “it’s to have more oxygen”. This idea is now largely abandoned. Modern explanations are more interesting.
Experiments have shown that increasing oxygen in the air does not prevent yawning. Lower the carbon dioxide a bit either. So yawning is not a simple “catching up for air”.
A strong lead today: yawning helps **regulate brain temperature**. By inhaling widely and stretching the face, we will “ventilate” and cool the head a little, especially when we are tired.

blocks.caption: Seeing someone yawn is often enough to trigger the reflex.

blocks.text: In humans, seeing, hearing, or even reading the word “yawn” can trigger a yawn. It's not just a stupid imitation: it also affects **empathy** and brain circuits linked to , neurons that activate when we act... or when we see someone act. [[Mirror neurons and contagiousness]]
Young children yawn little due to contagion. This sensitivity comes later, along with certain social skills.

sections.title: We already yawn before we are born

blocks.text: Fetuses yawn from around the **11th week** of pregnancy. At this age, their lungs do not yet breathe air. So, again, it's not about "running out of oxygen."
In the fetus, yawning could help the development of jaw and facial muscles.
We often yawn when we are tired... but also just before a test, or when we are bored while trying to stay focused. Stretching may stimulate the nervous system and help **stay alert**.
Yawning is probably not a lack of oxygen. It would rather serve to regulate the brain (temperature, vigilance) and, in humans, it also spreads by social contagion.
